questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral using tabular integration: ∫π to 2π sin(x) dx
questions.solution: To evaluate the definite integral using tabular integration, integrate the function and evaluate it at the limits of integration. The antiderivative of sin(x) is -cos(x). So, ∫sin(x) dx = -cos(x) + C. Evaluate at the limits: (-cos(2π)) - (-cos(π)) = 0.
questions.explanation: Tabular integration involves integrating the function and evaluating it at the limits to find the definite integral.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is forgetting to evaluate the antiderivative at both upper and lower limits, instead of just one. This would result in answer A (-2) which is incorrect.

questions.explanation: Tabular integration requires integrating the function and evaluating it at the limits to find the definite integral.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is not simplifying the antiderivative before plugging in the limits, which may lead to answers C (75) or D (90).

questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral using tabular integration: ∫-2 to 2 e^x dx
questions.solution: The antiderivative of e^x is e^x itself. So, ∫e^x dx = e^x + C. Evaluate at the limits: [e^2] - [-e^{-2}] = 0.
questions.explanation: Tabular integration involves integrating the function and evaluating it at the limits to find the definite integral.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is forgetting that e raised to an even power (like e^(-2)) will have a positive value, leading to answers A (e^2 - e^{-2}) or B (e^2 + e^{-2} - 2) which are incorrect.

questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral using tabular integration: ∫0 to π/2 cos(x) dx
questions.solution: The antiderivative of cos(x) is sin(x). So, ∫cos(x) dx = sin(x) + C. Evaluate at the limits: [sin(π/2)] - [sin(0)] = 1.
questions.explanation: Tabular integration requires integrating the function and evaluating it at the limits to find the definite integral.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is not remembering that sin(π/2) equals 1, which would lead to answers C (π/2) or D (π) which are incorrect.

questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral using tabular integration: ∫-1 to 1 x^3 dx
questions.solution: The antiderivative of x^3 is x^4/4. So, ∫x^3 dx = x^4/4 + C. Evaluate at the limits: [(1)^4/4] - [(-1)^4/4] = 0.
questions.explanation: Tabular integration involves integrating the function and evaluating it at the limits to find the definite integral.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is not recognizing that the function is odd, which means its definite integral over a symmetric interval will be zero. This would lead to answers B (1/4), C (1/2), or D (3/4) which are incorrect.

questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral using tabular integration: ∫-3 to 3 x^2 dx
questions.solution: The antiderivative of x^2 is x^3/3. So, ∫x^2 dx = x^3/3 + C. Evaluate at the limits: [(3)^3/3] - [(-3)^3/3] = 18 - (-18) = 9.
questions.explanation: Tabular integration requires integrating the function and evaluating it at the limits to find the definite integral.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is not simplifying the antiderivative before plugging in the limits, which may lead to answers C (18) or D (27).

questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral using tabular integration: ∫-4 to 4 sin(2x) dx
questions.solution: The antiderivative of sin(2x) is -1/2 cos(2x). So, ∫sin(2x) dx = -1/2 cos(2x) + C. Evaluate at the limits: [-1/2 cos(8)] - [-1/2 cos(-8)] = 0.
questions.explanation: Tabular integration involves integrating the function and evaluating it at the limits to find the definite integral.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is not realizing that the cosine function is even, so the values at -8 and 8 will be equal, leading to a zero result. This would lead to answers B (-2), C (2), or D (4) which are incorrect.
